text: Joshua Johnson: Going through life with a willingness to ask more questions
than you make statements?
Liberating.
Nothing that happens after the question is your responsibility.
Your responsibility is to have the curiosity, the integrity,
the thoughtfulness,
and the humility to ask what's on your mind
and not bite your tongue because, well, it might be uncomfortable,
well, what are they going to say?
Let that be their problem.
[Intersections]
[Joshua Johnson, Journalist]
[Blake Mycoskie, Social entrepreneur]
JJ: What if we shuffle the deck?
BM: I'm fine with that.
JJ: Alright.
OK, deck duly shuffled.
BM: OK, you go first now.
JJ: Alright, so I can own what I've done?
BM: Yeah, yeah, exactly.
JJ: Alright, first question.
Are we losing the ability to have real conversations?
BM: Hmm.
I don't think so, actually.
I think that with everything that's going on
from a technical perspective,
we are, at least in my friend group,
I'm finding that people are yearning for more and more intimacy, vulnerability,
you know, dinner parties,
like, I'm feeling a pendulum shift back
because I feel like people have been so digitally focused for so long.
And no, I don't feel that way at all.
JJ: I get that, and I think the pendulum is definitely shifting.
I guess when I read this, the editor in me is like,
well, what do you mean by real?
So I think for some folks,
just being able to text you when they’re freaking out
and just have that little human conversation is real connectivity
because it sort of paves the way for a more open conversation.
Some people aren’t ready to have the eye-to-eye,
face-to-face like, conversation,
but they could chat you up all day on WhatsApp
and that's about as real as they can get.
And I don't know, but I suspect some people kind of need
to be walked from digital and virtual into real world,
into real space, real time.
And maybe that's what's a "real" conversation for them.
It kind of pulls them towards something else.
BM: Yeah, and I also, I was just thinking,
I’m probably more exposed to that
because most of the work I do is in mental health now.
And so most of the people I’m talking to, it’s about their mental health
and their opening up about their mental health journeys.
And so I'm kind of predisposed to a lot of very vulnerable, very honest,
very raw conversations,
probably more than the general population.
JJ: I imagine that some people start to have those conversations,
their capacity for it grows and maybe their desire for it.
Like, once you get the benefit of like, oh, that's what that was, then --
BM: You want more of it.
JJ: You want more of it, and you find the facility with it.
For liability purposes,
I'm going to start with a gentle swish and flick.
BM: OK, this is good.
So many men feel lonelier than ever and don't know how to talk to one another.
Where do they start?
JJ: I think that they might have to start inward,
because if you're not comfortable saying, "Hey man,
I'm not sure how to connect to other people,"
that's a level of exposure I'm not sure some guys are ready for,
if you're already struggling to connect to other people.
I think for some men,
maybe that first conversation needs to be in the mirror
And be like, "Look, this is what my life is,
there's no use kidding myself.
Here's where I really am.
This is what's happening, this is what my social life is like,
this is what my romantic life is like,
this is how I see myself,
this is what I actually want."
And figure out if I had more connection,
what would that mean to me?
What would a perfect day in my life look like
if I had the connections I wanted?
Rather than just, “Well you should reach out more.
You should be more connected."
Why? To what end?
I think a lot of guys, that I know anyway,
rebel against that because they're not sure
like, when you're done,
like, when do I know if this works?
Just kind of sitting in the discomfort and like, "OK, am I social now?"
Like, "Am I human now?"
It just feels too fuzzy.
So maybe the first thing they need to do is get it clear in here
so that they have a sense of agency.
When they're asked to go do something,
they can go, "That's not really what I'm looking for"
and mean it as opposed to, “Oh, do that.”
Like, “My goal is to make this change in my life
that would look this way
and that doesn't seem like it meets this goal
so I'm going to pass."
A little more actively than just being
kind of like, blown sideways through.
"You should be more social for socializing sake,"
you know what I mean?
BM: Yeah, I mean, I was thinking of it just like a very practical tip.
If someone is lonely
and they don't know how to talk to another man,
I think the easiest thing is to invite someone to coffee
and ask them about their life.
Because I find that if someone is hesitant or scared
or doesn't know how to be vulnerable with another man,
it's much easier if someone has gone first.
But if you really are feeling the need to do that,
then by inviting someone to coffee, you know,
ideally someone you have been close to before,
and just saying, "Hey, I just want to check in,"
like, "How is everything going in your life?"
That guy is most likely going to share
and then that will make it easier for then you to share.
So I guess I’m going to [answer] this question
much more practical [than] someone watching this right now.
They’re like, “Man, I feel like I don’t have any good guy friends anymore.
I don't feel like I'm connected to my buddies at all."
And actually, I have a short little story about this,
which is interesting.
I was on my way home for Thanksgiving and I went home,
and I was at the time -- gosh, it was 19 years ago.
So I was like 29, 30 years old.
And I said, "Dad, after Thanksgiving, can we go into the study
and I want to interview you about your life."
My dad was like, "OK," we were close.
And so I asked my dad all these questions about his life,
and it was just a great experience.
But at the end, I asked him that final question.
I said, "Dad, [do] you have any regrets?"
And he said, "Blake, I do have one regret."
I said, "OK, what is it?"
He said, "Look, your mom and I
have had this beautiful marriage for now, 37 years.
You, your sister and your brother have turned out great.
You're all doing different things and following your passion.
I've loved my medical practice and helping people.
But over the years, I really lost touch with all my guy friends.
You know, all my friends from college, all my friends from medical school.
You know, I always just said no
to the weekend golf guys trips or to this or that,
because I was just so busy with you and your mom and my work.
And now you guys are in college or out of the house.
You know, I'm now getting close to retirement.
And I love your mom, but I can't spend every moment with her.
And so I don't really have anyone to hang out with.
And I'm lonely."
And he said, "So don't make that mistake."
And so at that time, I was 30 years old.
I had just started Toms Shoes -- we were like two years old.
And I wrote an email to my seven best friends --
a couple of them from college, some were newer friends in LA --
and I told them the story, and I said,
"We can't have this happen to us.
Let's do an annual trip every year."
And so we started our first trip 19 years ago,
and we're getting ready to have our 20th anniversary.
JJ: Where was the first trip?
BM: The first trip was a camping and fishing trip in Colorado.
And we've done one trip every single year for 19 years.
The group is now 14 guys.
We call it the “Rugged Adventure Club.”
It was rugged,
and then when I sold Toms, it became not so rugged.
We started going to the Maldives and all these places.
JJ: You can't call it like, "the guys who glamp," it doesn't ring.
BM: Exactly.
But I bring that up because, you know,
that group has taught me how to have really meaningful,
deep relationships with men,
which has had probably as big of an impact
on my mental health as anything else.
JJ: I love that story because your dad had the presence of mind
and the willingness to be vulnerable with his regrets.
Can I tell you my version of that story?
BM: Sure, I'm here for it.
JJ: My father, you know,
my father passed away last year and was ill for a very long time.
His health declined, declined, declined, declined for years.
And he and I were really quite estranged.
You know, he and my mother divorced when I was five,
the estrangement deepened after I came out.
And so it was just kind of like a process.
And my father was a Jehovah's Witness,
so it was just one thing after another.
Eventually I kind of felt convicted and I was like,
I need to keep trying to reach out.
And I tried to reach out and tried to reach out.
Finally, kind of in the last year of his life,
he was really not doing well.
And I thought, I need to make time to fly home to Florida
and just sit down and talk to the guy.
And I said, "Dad, I want to do your oral history.
I feel like I don't know you.
Like, not really know you."
Made a special trip, planned the whole thing.
"Dad, are we still going to do this?"
"Yup, I'll see you in three days."
I flew down, checked in the hotel, got up the next day, went to visit my mom,
"Dad, are we still on?"
"Yep, I'll see you."
Another day: "Dad?" "Yep."
"Tomorrow. Do it."
The morning comes and I call him.
"OK, dad. I'm ready to go.
When should I come meet you?"
"You know ...
We've got time.
I don't want you to put yourself out
and, like, I'm not really feeling up to it.
Well don’t worry about it, but we’ve got time.”
It's like, "Dad, I booked a flight for you.
I bought equipment.
I'm ready to do this now."
"You know what?
Next time you come down, let me know."
BM: Oh, no.
JJ: "We'll do it then, we've got time."
BM: Oh, no.
JJ: And in that moment, I decided, I'm done.
I'm not going to ask anymore.
I don't know what it was,
but I think my father was unable
to really process being a dad
beyond being a provider.
And that human connection of like, "this is how to be a man,
this is how to be a Black man,"
never quite clicked for him, even after I became a storyteller.
He knew I was a journalist, very proud of my work,
but couldn’t quite get
[that] I don’t need what you can provide for me.
I need you.
And when he passed, I was supposed to like, write his obit.
Still haven't.
Because I don't know what to write.
BM: OK, so this question is great.
I'm assuming it's the one we're already having, but you tell me,
what's the most transformational conversation you've ever had?
JJ: Oh, God, I had so many.
I mean, I was an interviewer for a living,
so I've had way too many.
I think the biggest collection of transformational conversations
I ever had was when I was a national host on NPR.
I got to interview Eric Holder,
the former US Attorney General under Barack Obama.
And I was really excited to interview him because it was one of the first people
of his echelon that I had ever talked to.
I was really excited.
And then after a while,
I could kind of hear my goofy family in the background
because we're not highfalutin, we're not fancy people,
very together,
but we don’t put on airs and attitudes
and something about it felt weird.
Especially because I wasn't thinking anything about the guest after him.
It was nobody famous.
And so I decided to like, OK,
I'm just going to talk to him like he's any other guest.
Invite him in,
"How's it going? Have a seat."
Make comfortable, very personable guy.
Easy to talk to.
Segment starts.
Break comes.
His assistant comes in to remind him,
"Sir, we're going to leave halfway through the next segment."
We're going to play music and he was going to be able to slip out of the studio.
He looks over his shoulder at his assistant and is like,
"I think we can stay a few more minutes."
Extended the interview on the spot
because he was having a good time.
BM: Yeah, yeah.
JJ: And I was, you know, smelling myself for a second, like,
"That's right, I'd extended it with me too."
But then after it was over, I thought like, dang, I made the right choice.
And from that,
I kind of reframed the way that I deal with just about everybody.
I mean, if you were going to treat every person you will ever meet
for the rest of your life exactly the same,
how would you treat them?
That's what that taught me.
Is to be one person, to set one standard, raise or lower,
some people you're going to embrace,
and some people are going to drive you up the wall.
But it sort of made every interview that followed easier
because I didn't have to calibrate myself.
It’s like conversation no longer depended on anything around me.
It depended on everything within me.
Like I know who I am as a person,
I know what my values are,
I know how I want to be treated.
That rule is golden for a reason.
And I decided that's who I'm going to be.
And if we don't vibe, that's cool.
If we do, that's fine.
But it just made life so much easier and it made the work easier.
Like, this is me.
Oh, we don't click? OK, cool, that's cool.
You get to be you, I get to be me.
And we figure it out somewhere along the way.
And through all of the ups and downs
of talking to all kinds of different people,
that was just like,
it just greased the wheels for the next three years of that work.
It was ...
I'm amazed I thought of it.
I didn't know I was that bright.
I'm glad I had that burst of insight because it made life so much simpler,
so much simpler.
BM: I love that, I love that.
OK, so for me,
what's the most transformational conversation you've ever had?
It actually happened about a year ago, with my kids.
And I have an 11-year-old and an eight-year-old.
And also a 31-year-old adopted son.
But this was with the biological kids.
And they had seen, you know,
and experienced me having a really hard mental health crisis
for about two years.
I was in and out of treatment centers,
I wasn't able to kind of, be there for them
in the way that I was before, it was a really hard time.
And then I started feeling better.
I had some amazing healing experiences,
especially around this core wound of not feeling enough.
And as I started feeling better, they could tell it was really different.
And now I'm spending a lot more time with them.
And the conversation I had with them is one day,
my son said something about like, "What's different?"
And kind of like, well,
"How do we know you're not going to feel bad again" type thing?
He was worried.
I said, “Because now I know that I’m enough,
just as I am."
Not because of what I've done, not because of what I built,
not because of what everyone thinks of me,
but just because I exist.
And now that I know that,
I think my life will always be different.
And I saw him like, look.
And it was the coolest thing
because I then continued the conversation like,
"And that extends to you and your sister too.
You guys are enough exactly as you are.
You can try out for the water polo team,
you can try to make good grades,
You can try to do these things.
But none of that is tied to your worth.
I love you, and your mom loves you and the world loves you.
And they always will just because you exist."
And ever since then, I've seen a lightness in my kids
and a connection in us
that is so deep, so peaceful,
so much that at dinner every night we have this little ritual
where we hold hands and my eight-year-old,
we start with the youngest first, and she says, "I am enough,"
and looks around and then she looks at us,
she goes, "You are enough,"
and she goes, "And we are enough."
And then the next child does it, and then I do it.
And that all came from that conversation.
And I hadn't even thought about that until this.
But it was one of probably the most important conversations of my life.
JJ: Two questions I have to ask on that.
When you said you saw a lightness in your kid,
was there anything in particular that you were concerned about
getting heavy for them?
Like, were there certain aspects of growing up
that you thought they needed that message for?
BM: I think when someone does not feel enough,
which I didn't for 48 years of my life,
then I think you subconsciously project that onto others
and especially parents to kids.
So if a parent doesn't feel enough
and doesn't have their own sense of worth outside of their accomplishments,
then you're projecting that pressure onto the kids.
So I think my son was feeling like he had to become a great water polo player,
or had to be the star of the basketball team,
or had to make great grades,
or had to look a certain way because I felt that about myself.
I never said that to him.
JJ: You don't have to say it.
BM: I didn't have to say it.
But as soon as I felt that I was enough and I said that to them,
then I saw him reduce the pressure he was putting on himself.
And my daughter still, I think, has somewhere to grow in that,
because I still think she puts a lot of pressure on herself still.
I mean, she's only eight.
But I have seen that when we do the ritual at dinner,
there's like a twinkle in their eye, there's a smile,
there's like, "Yeah, I am enough."
And it's a practice.
It's not something like,
oh, I experienced it once and now I have it forever.
It's something that you have to continue to practice every day.
You know, that's why I wear the bracelet.
It's my reminder every day to go back to this centering.
But that conversation with the kids,
I think will be one that I'm willing to bet any amount of money
if they're sitting in these chairs someday,
at least my son would say
that was probably the most meaningful conversation.
JJ: I see you have two of those bracelets,
and I feel like when you said enough --
BM: You know why I have two?
JJ: Why?
BM: You'll see. So one of my favorite things to do,
it's not about wearing it yourself.
It's about giving it to someone else.
So I always wear an extra one.
So if I ever feel like, OK,
this is something I want to share with someone,
which I do right now, I can give it.
So hold out your hand, palm up.
There you go.
And it says "you are enough" on the inside.
JJ: Oh, wow.
BM: And then ...
Now you have one, too.
JJ: I love it, thank you.
BM: You're welcome.
JJ: Thank you so much.
When I saw this, I kind of saw this
with a period and also with an exclamation point.
BM: It can be both.
JJ: Like, enough!
As sort of a check point.
BM: Boundary.
JJ: Or enough, like a relief almost.
BM: It's interesting you bring that up because I originally made it,
we hand-make them, these women in India make them.
And that's where I had a bunch of my healing.
And originally, it was more the "I am enough," a softness.
But I also think in the climate that we live in today,
there is something also that's a real activist spirit.
So it's like, enough!
And almost even like, I think of,
you know, people who sometimes have been told [in] their life
that they're not smart enough or pretty enough
or that they're going to amount to enough.
It's almost like a "fuck you" to all the people
who said you couldn't do it,
that you are enough and you don't need their validation.
JJ: I love it.
Thank you for this.
BM: OK, let's see.
Where did that go?
JJ: Right.
It's the daily double.
No.
If you could redesign how people connect with each other,
where would you start?
BM: If I could --
JJ: Wait. You went somewhere.
Where did you go?
BM: This is exactly where I went.
I went to "Avatar."
JJ: I knew there was something specific.
BM: And Pandora.
And if you've watched "Avatar,"
when the Avatar gets on the horse, then they plug in the hair --
JJ: Yeah.
BM: So that's where I went.
JJ: Where they kind of like --
BM: Yeah. And then I was like, if I could design any way to connect,
there'd be some way that like, when we shook hands,
I transferred part of my consciousness to you.
And so we connected in a nonverbal way.
And we could have conversation through touch
without having to use our words.
That's where I just went.
JJ: But, you know, I get it.
I knew you saw something specific.
I could see your eyes moving behind your eyebrows.
If I could redesign how people connect,
I would make it an educational prerequisite.
I would put it into schools because that's within our power.
I would put listening, communication,
and critical thinking as a high school graduation requirement.
BM: Yeah, beautiful.
JJ: I would make it a Common Core standard.
I would put it in the Common Core,
especially because when you’re little,
like, kids [have] great questions.
Kids are built-in question-askers,
idea finder-outers and they’re heuristic learning machines
and they'll pepper you with a million questions.
But that's exactly where, as a living thing,
your first job is to connect.
The first thing a baby does is connect with its mother.
And so, connection is our lifeblood.
And I think if you start real young,
I mean, I did speech and debate in middle and high school.
[The] best skill set I ever learned --
as much as I use math and science, writing, social studies --
the best skill set I ever learned was how to communicate with other people,
because that's how you connect.
Every piece of the social crisis we see with young people --
computers and AI and TikTok --
it all comes back to human connection.
They're trying to connect, but you can't do it 14 seconds at a time.
You've got to sort of invest in it.
And I think kids are sort of crying out for it.
They know something's wrong.
They know that their parents and grandparents did not go through this,
but they don't know why they have to.
They’re aware of what’s happening,
and frankly, are already starting to get a little scared about it.
I read a study last week that said Gen Z is saving for retirement
at higher rates than baby boomers did at their age.
So they're aware the world is not built for them right now,
and they're going to want to find solace in one another.
I think if we teach kids to do it, they'll stick to it.
They'll learn what appropriate conversations are,
listening, investing in people, even eye contact.
Even just something as simple as you and me being able
to look at each other and have the conversation
and not feel like, you know, we're either staring each other down
or like, waiting for one of our heads to explode.
That skill set for kids is just ...
It revolutionizes what it's like to grow up
and to become a citizen of the world.
I would start by making it a Common Core standard
and making it a high school requirement in schools.
BM: That's great, I love it.
JJ: Now I'm going to throw it where I ain't supposed to throw it
and see if it ends up where it's supposed to be.
BM: Oh!
JJ: See that?
BM: OK, that was good.
JJ: They set you up for failure and you find success.
BM: OK, we only have two left.
Here we go.
JJ: But first, let's see the one you didn't pick.
I'll ask you and you can put the answer in the comments.
How about that?
The one we didn't pick.
When did you realize that strength and vulnerability
were not opposites?
Put it in the comments.
BM: So the last question today is,
what are some tips you have to help others have deeper conversations?
JJ: That is a perfect question to end on.
I shuffled the deck and it landed the right way.
You're welcome.
Tips to have deeper conversations?
I would get really good at asking questions.
And I'll give you one example.
I used to be in public radio,
and when I started to get on the air and people noticed me, they would --
it happened over and over --
"Oh, you're Joshua Johnson?
Oh, I never would have guessed you were Bla --
Tall! I never would have thought you were so tall.
You sound three-foot-nine on the radio."
Happened over and over and it used to make me crazy.
And I finally figured out a simple two-word response
that changed everything.
Not those two words.
When they would say,
"I never would have guessed you were Black."
My response was,
why not?
And pause and don't say anything.
BM: That's what one of my tips is going to be,
be very comfortable with silence.
JJ: Well and here's the thing.
What I finally learned was, there's nothing I can say to you
that will hurt more than what you will say to yourself.
And when they reflect back to themselves,
why they actually said that,
they went, "Oh my God, I'm so sorry."
And I say, "It's OK, but now you know,
and now you can decide if that's the person you want to be.
But it's not my problem anymore.
It's your problem."
And that gave me peace, I could let it go,
I didn't have to walk through life like,
"I can't believe these white people, the way they treat us,
we ain't never gonna rise."
And I didn't have to --
babies don’t sleep that well.
And I think the right question,
plus the confidence to stand on the question
and just let it sit,
whatever the response is.
And so going through life with a willingness
to ask more questions than you make statements?
Liberating.
Nothing that happens after the question is your responsibility.
Your responsibility is [to]
have the curiosity, the integrity,
the perspicacity, the thoughtfulness,
and the humility to ask what's on your mind
and not bite your tongue because,
"Well, it might be uncomfortable," "What are they going to say?"
Let that be their problem.
I have a question for you.
"Is it OK if I ask, or did you just need to be heard?
Is it OK if I put this out there?
Or is now not the good time?"
"OK, sure, ask."
Say it and then stand on it.
Makes life much, much easier.
BM: OK, great.
I think that deep conversations require time.
I think that if you really want to have a deep conversation,
you need to have undistracted time.
And it's kind of a little bit of what you said around
ask the question and then be comfortable being silent
because it's in the pause where the depth can come out.
And I think that so much of our conversations with people,
the reason why they're not deep
is because we're always pressed for time
and our attention is always scattered.
And so in order to have deep conversations,
that's why I love hosting this podcast now,
because I know that the person has set aside two hours.
And I might only have an hour's worth of questions for them,
but I'm not in any rush, you know.
And so when I ask the question, I have plenty of time
to allow them to go deeper.
And then often, also what you said I liked
is like, asking a clarifying question
around the first question.
So not just jumping to the next question,
but then asking a question that helps them go deeper.
And then sitting and having the time.
So I guess it really is about making sure
that there's enough time for the person to go deep.
JJ: Blake, thank you, sir, and thank you for this.
This is fantastic. I really appreciate it.
BM: Thank you so much, it was awesome.
